Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: The Courtauld Gallery, London, United Kingdom - Museum Tour
Tour-Category: museum

Stop 1: Paul Cézanne

Coordinates: 51.5113, -0.1162

The Courtauld Gallery is an art museum in Somerset House, on the Strand in central London. It houses the collection of the Samuel Courtauld Trust and operates as an integral part of the Courtauld Institute of Art. The Courtauld Gallery is home to one of the greatest collections of art in the UK and an annual programme of focused exhibitions, displays and contemporary commissions.

The Courtauld Gallery is open Monday to Sunday from 10:00 to 18:00. Admission is 11 pounds for adults; children 18 and under go free.

Orientation: From this vantage, the clarity of the figure and the subtle play of light across the surface become apparent—details that dissolve if viewed from too far or at an angle. The careful division of color, a hallmark of Seurat’s pointillist method, reveals itself only at close range, where the surface vibrates with countless deliberate touches.

Pause at the midpoint of the gallery, where the light falls directly onto Cézanne’s Apples, Bottle and Chairback and reveals the shifting textures of oil paint along the curved line of the chair. From here, the layering of shapes—apples, bottle, and the gentle arch of the chairback—emerges in dialogue, each form both distinct and slightly unsettled. The oil paint is handled in broad, deliberate strokes, with colors layered to create both weight and instability—apples appear to teeter, the bottle stands almost askew, and the chairback curves unexpectedly into the space of the table. Rather than offering a fixed viewpoint, Cézanne relies on a shifting sense of perspective. This approach, developed late in his career, blurred the boundaries between foreground and background, setting the stage for later artists to rethink how form and space could be constructed. Each object here feels both solid and provisional, a record of observation and revision. The effect is not of tranquility but of curiosity—the viewer’s eye moves restlessly, tracing the ways Cézanne constructed and deconstructed the everyday. This painting stands within The Courtauld’s collection as evidence of an artist reaching for something new in the final year of his life, inviting others to push the boundaries of form even further.

Ambroise Vollard, an art dealer and gallery owner in Paris, organized the first solo exhibition of Cézanne’s work in 1895. This shifted Cézanne’s reputation from an obscure figure among fellow artists to a name recognized in the wider art world. Courtauld transferred these works to establish The Courtauld Gallery's collection. As a result, The Courtauld Gallery now holds the most important group of Cézanne's works in Britain, showcasing them to the public and cementing its status as a key institution for Cézanne's art. These masterpieces showcase the evolution of modern art techniques and offer a glimpse into the exploration of the human psyche. As you traverse these pieces, immerse yourself in the artistic minds of these renowned creators, each contributing uniquely to the narrative of modern art.

Directions: Continue through The Courtauld Gallery — next is Georges Seurat.

Stop 2: Georges Seurat

Coordinates: 51.5113, -0.1162

In the waning years of the nineteenth century—Seurat’s brief lifetime marked by the dates 1859-1891—this painting emerged as part of an epochal experiment. The canvas before you is rendered in oil, built up with the meticulous dots and dashes of chromoluminarism, the technique Seurat devised to harness the science of optics and color. Here, a young woman sits at her toilette, absorbed in the act of self-adornment. The composition is poised, almost architectural: a mirror reflects the scene, multiplying the reality, while the palette of pale pinks and gentle creams is not mixed but laid side by side in discrete points. This method, known as pointillism, was radical at the time, as it demanded that the viewer complete the image optically, merging the colors in the eye rather than on the palette. Seurat’s artistic temperament was marked by a rare duality—extreme sensitivity entwined with a passion for logical abstraction. The result is an image that feels both intimate and remote, a private moment constructed with scientific detachment. Yet in “ ” the domestic replaces the maritime, and the quiet act of self-decoration becomes a vessel for Seurat’s larger questions about perception and reality. Samuel Courtauld, the industrialist and collector whose trust now holds this work, sought out Seurat’s paintings precisely because they marked a turning point in the understanding of color and vision. Courtauld’s acquisitions brought together the largest collection of Seurat’s work in the United Kingdom, making this gallery a locus for studying the painter’s restless pursuit of unity between emotion and logic. Standing here, the painting’s effect is one of suspended time: each dot is a moment, each patch of color a measure of patience and intent. Seurat’s method does not simply record the passing of a day; it holds time still, challenging the viewer to experience the world as a constellation of sensations assembled in the mind. The human cost was real—this was the work of a life cut short, ambitions left unfinished, a new vision glimpsed but not fully realized. What remains is wonder: the quiet radiance of a scene both ordinary and transformed, and the unanswerable question of how an artist’s internal struggle is made visible in the surface of paint.

Directions: Your final stop in The Courtauld Gallery: Vincent van Gogh’s  Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear.

Stop 3: Vincent van Gogh’s  Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear

Coordinates: 51.5113, -0.1162

Orientation: As you stand before Vincent van Gogh’s Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear, position yourself so that the brushwork is visible along the line where the bandage meets the fur cap—it’s here that the texture of the paint and the thickness of the strokes show how van Gogh worked quickly, layering color to capture both the cold of Arles in January and the immediacy of his condition.

Vincent van Gogh painted Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear in January 1889 in Arles, France. In the weeks after suffering a severe personal crisis, he produced this oil-on-canvas portrait, measuring 60 by 49 centimeters. The painting shows van Gogh turned three-quarters, his left ear wrapped in a white bandage and covered by a fur hat to fend off the winter. His face appears pale and tense, and his eyes—set against the strong verticals of the background—are rimmed with fatigue and something more difficult to name. The fur cap, rendered in deep, dark strokes, presses down over the thick white bandage, while his coat—broad, blocky, almost sculpted in green and blue—envelops him against the chill.

This work marked a pivotal episode in van Gogh’s life. He had just left hospital treatment, and the incident with his ear became a turning point that left him isolated but compelled to keep painting. Van Gogh chose to show himself not at his best, but in the aftermath of crisis, painting directly onto canvas at a moment when most would have retreated. What remains is a portrait that records not only a likeness, but also the price and persistence of creation under strain—a self-reflection that changed what portraiture could risk or reveal.

This tour highlights the evolution of modern art through innovative techniques and the personal struggles of artists, exemplified by van Gogh’s Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear. Their works encourage us to reflect on the transformative power of creativity in the face of adversity. That's 3 stops in all.
